comments.title: He Had No Lawyer. So He Wrote the Supreme Court in Pencil.
comments.text: Gideon's petition was written in pencil, on prison stationery, and the Court took it. Today an appointed lawyer in some counties carries over 200 felony files at once. If you have ever actually been assigned one, how much time did you get with them?

comments.title: The Police Broke In - So the Court Let Her Go
comments.text: The evidence against Dollree Mapp was real. It was thrown out because of how it was found. That rule means a guilty person can sometimes walk because an officer skipped a step. Which step do you think should never be skippable?

comments.title: The Hidden Code Door Behind the $8 Billion FTX Fraud
comments.text: Ordinary FTX customers could not go negative. Alameda had an exemption written into the code. Which failure is worse in your book - the person who wrote that line, or the auditors and investors who never asked to see it?

comments.title: He warned regulators about Madoff for nearly ten years
comments.text: Harry Markopolos handed the SEC the arithmetic in 2000 and again in 2005, and nothing happened until 2008. If you had done the maths and been ignored twice by the regulator, what would your next move have been?

comments.title: Police Can Stop and Frisk You Without Arresting You
comments.text: Terry lets an officer pat someone down on reasonable suspicion - less than probable cause, more than a hunch. If you have been frisked, were you told the reason at the time? I am curious how often that actually happens.

comments.title: Police Took His Phone. Then They Opened It.
comments.text: Before Riley, a phone at arrest was treated like a wallet: openable on the spot. The Court said a phone is different because of what it holds. If a phone is different, is the car it was sitting in different too, or not?

comments.title: The phone in his pocket testified against him for months
comments.text: 127 days of Timothy Carpenter's movements came from his carrier, not from him. Records a company keeps about you - whose are they? Say where you would draw that line and why.

comments.title: Read Rights or It's Out | Miranda v. Arizona
comments.text: Miranda warnings are read thousands of times a day and usually waived within minutes. Does a right explained in eight seconds, in handcuffs, actually function as one? If you have heard them read for real, what did it sound like?

comments.title: Police Took His $42,000 Car. The Supreme Court Drew a Line.
comments.text: Tyson Timbs's Land Rover was worth about $42,000. The maximum fine for what he did was $10,000. At what ratio does taking property stop being a fine and start being a punishment - 2x, 4x, or does the ratio not matter?

comments.title: Your Home for a Developer? The Kelo Supreme Court Case
comments.text: New London took the houses, the developer never built, and the land sat empty for years. If the promised jobs never arrive, should the owners get their land back? What would that rule actually look like in writing?

comments.title: Can Your School Punish You for a Post You Made Off Campus?
comments.text: B.L. posted on a Saturday, off campus, from her own phone, and was cut from the team for it. Where does a school's authority stop - the property line, the school day, or something else? Parents here, I want your line specifically.

comments.title: The Fine Print That Quietly Took Your Right to Sue
comments.text: Almost every account you hold has an arbitration clause you agreed to without reading. Has anyone here ever actually gone through arbitration with a company? How did it go - almost nobody ever does it, so I would like a real account.

comments.title: The Supreme Court Let Police Take Your DNA at Arrest
comments.text: The Court compared a DNA swab at arrest to taking fingerprints. A fingerprint identifies one person; DNA describes their relatives too. Is that comparison fair, or is it doing too much work?

comments.title: He Drove Home Honking. The Police Followed Him Inside.
comments.text: Lange was honking with the music up - a misdemeanour - and the officer followed him into his own garage. Should a minor offence be enough to cross a front door, or should the offence have to be serious first?

comments.title: Behind the $9 billion promise was a machine that failed
comments.text: Every start-up promises something it cannot do yet. Holmes went to prison for it. Where is the actual line between 'fake it till you make it' and fraud - is it the patient, the investor, or what she knew when she said it?

comments.title: He called safety pure waste and dove anyway
comments.text: OceanGate's director of marine operations put his safety concerns in writing in 2018 and was fired. If you had been the one holding that document, what would you have done next - and honestly, would anyone have listened?

comments.title: There Was No Coin: $4 Billion in Empty Promises
comments.text: OneCoin took in billions with no blockchain behind it at all. What is the one thing an ordinary buyer could have checked in 2016 that would have exposed it? Genuinely asking - most of the usual advice would not have worked.

comments.title: The Day $1 Trillion Vanished in 36 Minutes
comments.text: Sarao traded from his parents' house and the US extradited him, while regulators listed several causes for the crash. Was he the cause, or the one person it was practical to charge?

comments.title: He sold a side door into America's best universities
comments.text: The parents went to prison. The universities kept the buildings donated by other wealthy families. Which is the real scandal here - the side door, or the front door that was always open?

comments.title: Two men dressed as police emptied a Boston museum
comments.text: The frames still hang empty in the Gardner and the $10 million reward has never been claimed. After 35 years, do you think those paintings still exist? Give me the reasoning, not just the guess.

comments.title: Fifty years later the FBI still cannot name him
comments.text: Cooper jumped into a storm at night with $200,000, and part of that money turned up on a riverbank in 1980. Did he survive? Which single piece of evidence settles it for you?

comments.title: One banker was paid $550 million in a single year
comments.text: Milken pleaded to six counts, none of them insider trading, paid a record penalty, and was later pardoned. Was junk-bond finance the crime, or the thing that made him worth prosecuting?

comments.title: The website he took from never wanted him charged
comments.text: JSTOR, the party he took from, declined to pursue it. Prosecutors filed 13 felony counts anyway. Should a victim who does not want charges be able to stop a prosecution? Yes or no, and where does that break down?

comments.title: A billionaire heard his own voice on an FBI tape
comments.text: This was the first big insider-trading case built on wiretaps, a tool written for organised crime. Was that proportionate? If not wiretaps, how would you prove a conversation happened at all?

comments.title: Can the Police Scan Your Home From the Street?
comments.text: The agent never set foot on Kyllo's property - he read the heat coming off the walls from a public street. Every year there are more sensors that can do that. Should the rule follow the property line, or the technology?

comments.title: The FBI taped a microphone to a phone booth roof
comments.text: Katz pulled the booth door shut, and the Court held that was enough to expect privacy. What is the 2026 equivalent of closing that door? I am not sure one exists any more - tell me if you think it does.

comments.title: The Traffic Stop Was Over. Then the Dog Arrived.
comments.text: The warning was written and handed back. The dog arrived seven or eight minutes later. Once a stop is finished, how long should an officer be allowed to hold you - zero minutes, eight, or does it depend on what?

comments.title: Their Son Was Charged. The City Came for His Parents' House.
comments.text: The Sourovelises were never charged with anything, and Philadelphia moved to take their house over about $40 of drugs their son sold. Should property be forfeitable when no person is convicted? If yes, on what proof?

comments.title: Alabama kept a date to kill him for 30 years
comments.text: Hinton spent 30 years on death row largely because his defence could not afford a competent ballistics expert. What is the fix - money for experts, or no death penalty at all? Pick one and say why the other fails.

comments.title: She memorized her attacker's face to be certain
comments.text: Jennifer Thompson deliberately memorised her attacker's face so she would be certain. She was certain, and she was wrong. What should a jury be told before it hears a confident identification?

comments.title: Police Can Force Your Thumb - But Maybe Not Your Mind
comments.text: Courts have generally allowed police to compel a thumb but not a passcode. Same phone, same contents. Does that distinction hold up for you, or is it a technicality that will not last?

comments.title: Police Can Search Your Car Without a Warrant - Except One Place
comments.text: A car can be searched with no warrant; the motorcycle parked up by the house could not. Before watching, would you have guessed where that line falls? What makes a driveway different from a street?

comments.title: The county sold her condo and kept the extra $25,000
comments.text: Hennepin County sold Geraldine Tyler's condo over a tax debt and kept every dollar of the surplus. Before this case a dozen states allowed that. Do you know what your state's rule is? Worth ten minutes to find out.

comments.title: They Took His Life Savings at the Airport - No Charges, No Crime
comments.text: Carrying cash is legal, and the government took it at the gate without charging anyone. Knowing that, how much cash would you now be willing to carry through a US airport? Put a number on it.

comments.title: Following the deposit rule is what made her a suspect
comments.text: Carole Hinders deposited under $10,000 because that is what a cash-only restaurant takes in, and that pattern is what made her a suspect. Is there any way to bank cash honestly that does not look like structuring?

comments.title: Thirty hours in jail because an algorithm chose his photo
comments.text: A face-recognition match put Robert Williams in a cell for 30 hours. Should a face match ever be enough to arrest on its own, or only enough to start looking? What would you require on top of it?

comments.title: He showed the officer the receipt and was arrested anyway
comments.text: Albert Florence had the receipt for the paid fine in the car and was arrested and strip-searched twice. Which failed first here - the officer, the database, or the rule that permitted the search?

comments.title: A Judge Took $2.8 Million to Send Kids to Prison
comments.text: Ciavarella's hearings ran about ninety seconds, many with no lawyer in the room, and thousands of parents watched it happen in person. Why do you think it took years before anyone stopped it?

comments.title: Police Are Allowed to Lie to You Until You Confess
comments.text: Police may legally invent evidence in an interrogation room. England banned the practice. Should the US? And if lying stays legal, what would have to change for a confession to be worth trusting?

comments.title: Police Destroyed His Home Chasing a Stranger - Then Paid Him Nothing
comments.text: Police wrecked the Lech family's house getting a stranger out of it, and the court held the city owed nothing because it was police power, not a taking. If not the homeowner, who should carry that bill?

comments.title: They Hid the Evidence That Proved Him Innocent
comments.text: A jury awarded John Thompson $14 million. The Supreme Court took all of it back, 5-4. If a prosecutor's office cannot be sued for hiding evidence, what is actually left that would deter it?

comments.title: Police Raided the Wrong House and Handcuffed an Innocent Woman
comments.text: Officers had the wrong address and Anjanette Young told them so 43 times. What should have to happen before a door goes in - a second confirmation, a supervisor's sign-off, a photograph of the door?

comments.title: Police Came for a Welfare Check and Left With His Guns
comments.text: His wife asked police to check he was alive. They took his guns with no warrant, and the Court said unanimously that community caretaking does not reach inside a home. Was that right for a case that began as a welfare check?

comments.title: Police Skipped His Rights - Then He Learned He Couldn't Even Sue
comments.text: After Vega v. Tekoh, an unread Miranda warning can cost the prosecution the statement, but you cannot sue the officer over it. Does a right you cannot sue over still work as a right, or is it something else now?

comments.title: She Was Jailed Because She Was Too Poor to Pay a Fine
comments.text: Montgomery jailed Harriet Cleveland to sit out about $1,554 in traffic fines. Debtors' prisons were abolished, and this is not called one. What would you call it?

comments.title: Police Never Saw the Driver - the Supreme Court Let Them Stop Him Anyway
comments.text: The deputy never saw who was driving. He assumed the registered owner was, and that assumption is now enough to pull you over. What one extra fact should an officer need before that stop is allowed?

comments.title: The Stop Was Illegal - the Supreme Court Kept the Evidence Anyway
comments.text: The stop was illegal, but an outstanding warrant found during it saved the evidence. Does that give an officer a reason to stop people and hope something turns up? If you would change the rule, change it in one sentence.

comments.title: Your School Can Search You Without a Warrant
comments.text: A school can search a student's bag on reasonable suspicion, no warrant needed. That bag now contains a phone. Should the same standard cover the phone? Teachers and parents here, I want your answer particularly.

comments.title: She Was Handcuffed and Jailed Over a $50 Seatbelt Fine
comments.text: Gail Atwater's offence carried no jail time by law, and she was handcuffed in front of her children anyway. Should arrest ever be available for an offence that cannot end in jail? Yes or no, and what is the exception?

comments.title: Five Children Confessed to a Crime They Didn't Commit.
comments.text: Five boys confessed, and not one confession matched the scene or the others. Which single change to interrogation would have stopped it - recording, a lawyer in the room, or a hard time limit?

comments.title: He Paid $139,000 Cash. There Was No Mortgage.
comments.text: The Cardosos owned that house outright and a bank padlocked it anyway. Over a million falsified documents were filed, and one executive went to prison. Does that ratio look like enforcement to you?

comments.title: The Repair Money Was Due July 1. The Building Fell June 24.
comments.text: The 2018 survey said the waterproofing had already failed, not that it was failing. At what point should someone outside that building have had the power to order it emptied - and who should that person be?

comments.title: 6 Trials. 4 Death Sentences. 23 Years.
comments.text: The same prosecutor tried Curtis Flowers six times for the same crime. How many trials should a state get before it has to stop? Put a number on it and say what happens at that number.

comments.title: A Computer Invents a GBP 2,000 Debt.
comments.text: The Post Office investigated, charged and prosecuted its own sub-postmasters - roughly one a week for fifteen years. Should a company be allowed to bring criminal prosecutions at all? Britain still permits it.

comments.title: A Doctor Reports Police Torture in 1982.
comments.text: A jail doctor described electrical burns in a letter to the Superintendent in 1982, and nothing happened for years. If a doctor's written report does not stop it, what would have? Name the mechanism.

comments.title: 4 Sailors Confess to One Murder. The DNA Clears Each One.
comments.text: DNA excluded each sailor in turn, and the theory grew by one man each time to fit around it. At which exclusion should the case have been dropped - the first, or the fourth? Say which and why.
